response.report:
EXAM: Chest radiograph, one view, 2026-11-21
CLINICAL INDICATION: Emergency department. Shortness of breath. History of prostate cancer on hormone therapy. Portable film.
ORDERING PROVIDER: Dr. J. Marte, ED
COMPARISON: Chest radiograph, 2026-06-30. Note: the prior report text (PA chest. Heart size normal. Lungs clear.) does not mention the cardiac device, and the prior image shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a left chest wall cardiac device generator with transvenous leads. The radiologist should confirm that the prior report belongs to this prior image.
TECHNIQUE: Current is AP, labeled supine, portable, with lower lung volumes. Prior is PA, appears upright, with adequate inspiration. Projection, position and inspiration differ from the prior. Both studies appear mildly rotated. Comparison is limited.

LOOK AT FIRST:
- F1: Increased hazy and reticular opacity, right perihilar and mid zone (time-sensitive).
- F2: Increased hazy and reticular opacity, left perihilar and mid zone (time-sensitive).
- F9: Linear densities over the tracheal air column, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen that could be an endotracheal tube, an enteric tube or central line, or external tubing. Indeterminate. The two reads disagreed (one read indeterminate, one read new). Not confirmed on this image (time-sensitive).
- F3: Right basal opacity, indeterminate (time-sensitive).
- F7: Enlarged cardiac silhouette, indeterminate for change (listed in the look-first order, not flagged time-sensitive).

FINDINGS (systematic read, done blind to the indication):
- Airway / lungs: Trachea is roughly midline allowing for rotation. Lung volumes are low. Diffuse bilateral hazy and reticular opacity, most marked in the perihilar and mid zones (F1 right, F2 left), increased from the prior, which showed largely clear lungs with mildly prominent markings. This may reflect interstitial or alveolar fluid; other diffuse processes are not excluded. Supine position and lower volumes contribute to some of the difference, but the opacity extends above the basal zones. Right basal opacity partly obscuring the right hemidiaphragm (F3) and retrocardiac and left basal opacity obscuring the left hemidiaphragm (F4) are both indeterminate; low volumes and supine position may mimic or exaggerate basal opacity, and the two reads agreed on indeterminate. No pleural line is seen, but sensitivity is limited on a supine film. No discrete lung mass is seen, with limited assessment.
- Mediastinum / hila: Upper mediastinum looks wide on an AP supine film; width cannot be compared with the PA prior. Both hila are indistinct with surrounding hazy opacity.
- Pleura: Both costophrenic angles are hazy and both hemidiaphragms are partly obscured. Possible layering pleural effusion on the right (F5) and on the left (F6), both indeterminate. Each was recorded by one of the two reads. Amount and change cannot be judged against the upright prior.
- Heart: Cardiac silhouette is enlarged on both studies (F7). It looks larger on the current film, but the current film is AP supine with low volumes, which magnifies the heart. Heart borders are partly blurred by adjacent lung opacity. Indeterminate for change.
- Bones / soft tissue: No displaced rib fracture or definite sclerotic or destructive lesion is seen in the visible ribs, clavicles or spine at this resolution. No soft tissue gas. F10: mottled, heterogeneous density over the right glenoid and scapular neck region on the current film, indeterminate. It could be a projectional effect from arm position and the overlying ECG electrode, or altered bone texture. This finding came from the focused pass and was not part of the two blind reads. Source image review in PACS is needed. Devices: Left chest wall cardiac device generator with transvenous leads (coil over the right mediastinum, coiled lead over the lower heart, electrode markers over the left heart) (F8). Configuration is broadly similar to the prior allowing for projection, with no visible lead discontinuity at this resolution. F9: see LOOK AT FIRST. These linear densities are not present on the prior. External monitoring leads are present.

INTERVAL CHANGE:
- Changed: Increased bilateral perihilar and mid-zone hazy and reticular opacity (F1, F2). Linear densities over the trachea, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen are not present on the prior; their status is indeterminate because the reads disagreed (F9).
- Unchanged: Left chest wall cardiac device generator and lead configuration (F8), allowing for projection. Basal opacities (F3, F4), possible effusions (F5, F6), cardiac size (F7) and the right scapular density (F10) are not comparable across the differing projection and position, so no change is called.

RECIST 1.1: not computed on radiographs

CAN'T DETERMINE:
- Has the heart size changed? | Reason: Prior is PA and current is AP supine with low volumes. AP projection and low inspiration magnify the heart shadow. | Recommend: Repeat PA and lateral when the patient is able. Echocardiography if clinically relevant.
- Is the upper mediastinum widened? | Reason: The current film is AP supine with mild rotation, which widens the mediastinal shadow. Device leads cross the region. | Recommend: Repeat upright PA film when the patient is able, or CT chest if there is clinical concern.
- Are pleural effusions present, and have they changed? | Reason: The current film is supine, so fluid layers posteriorly and shows only as haze. The prior is upright. The amounts are not comparable. | Recommend: Upright or decubitus film, bedside ultrasound, or CT chest.
- Do the basal opacities reflect consolidation, collapse, layering fluid or low volumes? | Reason: Low inspiration and supine position crowd the lower zones and mimic basal opacity. The magnified heart hides the left base. | Recommend: Repeat film with good inspiration when the patient is able, or CT chest.
- Is there a pneumothorax? | Reason: No pleural line is seen, but on a supine film air collects anteriorly and at the bases and may not show. A skin fold or linen line and external wires cross the chest. | Recommend: Upright or decubitus film, or CT chest if there is clinical concern.
- Are an endotracheal tube, enteric tube or central line present, and where are the tips? | Reason: Linear densities over the trachea, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen overlap device leads, external wires and the spine. The image is low resolution. | Recommend: Review the source image in PACS with edge enhancement and correlate with the bedside record of lines and tubes. Confirm tip positions before use.
- Are there small lung nodules, or lesions behind the heart or generator? | Reason: Diffuse opacity on the current film, the device generator over the left upper chest and the enlarged heart all hide lung. The AP portable film is lower quality than the PA prior. | Recommend: CT chest if clinically relevant, or repeat PA and lateral after the diffuse opacity clears.
- Is there free gas under the diaphragm? | Reason: The current film is supine. Free gas does not collect under the diaphragm in this position. | Recommend: Upright or decubitus film if there is clinical concern.
- Is there a pleural effusion on either side, and has it changed? | Reason: The current film is supine, so fluid layers posteriorly and shows only as hazy density. Both costophrenic angles are indistinct on the current film and were clear on the upright PA prior. | Recommend: Upright or semi-erect film or decubitus views when the patient is able, or bedside ultrasound or CT chest.
- Is the upper mediastinum truly widened? | Reason: Supine AP projection with mild rotation widens the mediastinal shadow. The prior PA showed no widening. | Recommend: Repeat upright PA film when the patient is able, or CT chest if there is clinical concern.
- Is the right basal opacity consolidation, atelectasis or layering fluid? | Reason: Low lung volumes and supine position crowd the base and obscure the hemidiaphragm. A frontal film alone cannot separate these. | Recommend: Repeat film with better inspiration, upright if possible, or CT chest.
- Where exactly is the endotracheal tube tip relative to the carina, and is there an enteric tube with its tip in the stomach? | Reason: The image is low resolution and the carina is not clearly defined. A tubular density over the upper abdomen could be an enteric tube or external tubing. | Recommend: Review the source image in PACS with windowing. Repeat the film if the tube positions remain unclear.
- Are there small nodules or subtle bone lesions on either study? | Reason: The device generator overlies the left upper and mid zones on both films. Diffuse opacity and portable technique on the current film hide fine detail. | Recommend: CT chest if clinically indicated. Review source images in PACS.

IMPRESSION:
1. Increased bilateral hazy and reticular perihilar and mid-zone opacity compared with the prior (F1, F2). This may reflect interstitial or alveolar fluid; other diffuse processes are not excluded. Comparison is limited by AP supine technique, low volumes and different projection.
2. Linear densities over the trachea, right upper mediastinum and upper abdomen (F9) that could be an endotracheal tube, an enteric tube or central line, or external tubing. Indeterminate; the two reads disagreed. Presence and tip positions are not confirmed.
3. Right basal opacity (F3) and left retrocardiac and basal opacity (F4) are indeterminate; consolidation, collapse, layering fluid and low volumes cannot be separated.
4. Enlarged cardiac silhouette on both studies (F7). Change in size cannot be determined across PA and AP supine projections.
5. Possible bilateral pleural effusions (F5, F6), indeterminate. Pneumothorax and free subdiaphragmatic gas cannot be excluded on a supine film.
6. Mottled density over the right scapula and glenoid region (F10), indeterminate, in a patient with a history of prostate cancer. Source image review in PACS is needed.
7. Left chest wall cardiac device with transvenous leads, configuration similar to the prior (F8).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Repeat PA and lateral chest radiograph with good inspiration, upright, when the patient is able.
- Upright or decubitus chest film if there is clinical concern for pneumothorax, free gas or effusion. Bedside ultrasound for effusion.
- CT chest if clinically relevant, or for persistent concern about basal opacity, mediastinal width, effusion, pneumothorax or small nodules.
- Review source images in PACS with edge enhancement and windowing, including the right scapular density, lead integrity and tube or line positions. Correlate with the bedside record of lines and tubes and confirm tip positions before use.
- Echocardiography if clinically relevant for cardiac size.

AI DRAFT: requires resident review and attending signature.
